name: bigcommerce
_readme: BigCommerce as a TARGET only: multi-tenant Open SaaS with no inspectable shop code base - extension happens through apps, the Management (REST/GraphQL) APIs, webhooks, Scripts, Stencil themes and the GraphQL Storefront API (Catalyst as the headless starter). Seed from stable API-shape knowledge. No source role and no adapter.py: there is no server-side code base to scan.

as_target.default_frontend: Stencil theme (Cornerstone) as shipped; headless on the GraphQL Storefront API with Catalyst (Next.js) as the official starter

snippets.critic2_persona: senior solution architect who has delivered several BigCommerce projects on both Stencil and headless Catalyst, holds the BigCommerce developer/architect certifications, and knows precisely where the SaaS boundary sits - which plan unlocks a feature, what B2B Edition adds, and which requirements can only be met in an app or an external service
snippets.docs_domains: developer.bigcommerce.com (API reference for the V3/V2 Management APIs, the GraphQL Storefront API and the GraphQL Admin API, webhooks, Scripts, Widgets, Checkout SDK, app development and OAuth scopes, API rate limits per plan); support.bigcommerce.com (merchant-facing behaviour, plan feature matrix, Page Builder, Channel Manager, multi-storefront); catalyst.dev and github.com/bigcommerce/catalyst (the headless Next.js starter and its component set); developer.bigcommerce.com/theme-objects and github.com/bigcommerce/cornerstone (Stencil theme and the shipped widget set); developer.bigcommerce.com/b2b-edition for the separate B2B Edition APIs and buyer portal - B2B Edition has its own API host and its own docs tree, do not read it as part of the core V3 API.
snippets.best_practice: treat the platform as a black box: model every extension as an app (OAuth app with scopes, or a single-click app) plus an external service, never as a change to platform behaviour; keep catalog, price and inventory as the platform's system of record and push deltas through the V3 APIs in batches rather than record-by-record because rate limits are per plan and per store; use webhooks plus an idempotent consumer instead of polling; put storefront data fetching on the GraphQL Storefront API (customer-impersonation token for logged-in data) and never expose a Management API token to a browser; customise checkout through the Checkout SDK / Open Checkout or an embedded-checkout flow rather than expecting server-side checkout hooks; model each brand or market as a Channel/Site (multi-storefront) instead of separate stores when catalog and orders must stay unified.
snippets.critic2_focus: D1: which plan tier and which add-on a claimed capability needs (Enterprise vs Pro, B2B Edition as a paid add-on), current API versions (V3 vs the remaining V2 endpoints), and rate limits per plan. D2: is the claimed standard capability really native, or is it an app from the marketplace with its own licence and support model. D3: does the SaaS standard truly cover the requirement, or does it cover 80% with the remainder impossible because there is no server-side extension point - name the feature and the plan. D4: exact endpoint families and GraphQL fields, whether the data the frontend needs is available on the Storefront API at all (versus admin-only), which Page Builder widget renders the content and whether a headless frontend can render it, and whether the checkout customisation in scope is inside the Checkout SDK boundary.
snippets.expected_hotspots_d3: complex B2B beyond the B2B Edition buyer portal (multi-level company hierarchies, contract pricing rules, budgets and cost centres); customer-specific pricing at scale through price lists (list count, record volume and assignment logic); quote negotiation depth; punchout (OCI / cXML); ERP-driven live price and stock lookups per request; tax and compliance rules beyond the shipped/partner tax providers; complex bundles, configurable products and made-to-order options; document downloads per customer; search merchandising and faceting depth on large catalogs; workflow/approval logic, which has no server-side engine and must live in an external service; content personalisation, which needs an external system
snippets.expected_blockers_d4: API rate limits (per plan, per store) turn any per-request or per-record integration into a design problem - batch, cache and queue instead; limited server-side extensibility - there is NO place to run custom code inside the platform, so every rule, validation or enrichment beyond configuration must run in an app or an external service, with the latency and consistency cost that implies; checkout customisation is bounded by Open Checkout / the Checkout SDK / embedded checkout - server-side checkout logic, custom checkout steps with platform-side validation and custom payment flows outside the supported gateway set are the usual hard stops; multi-storefront and B2B depth (channel-scoped catalog, pricing, content and customer data are not uniformly channel-aware across every API - verify per resource); B2B Edition runs on its own API host and data model beside the core store, so company, quote and invoice data must be joined client-side or in middleware; Page Builder widgets are rendered by the Stencil theme, so a headless frontend must reimplement each widget it needs (Makeswift covers part of this - verify); Scripts API injection has no equivalent in a headless frontend; webhook delivery is at-least-once and unordered, so consumers must be idempotent; data migration has no import of historical orders with their original ids beyond what the V2/V3 order APIs accept
snippets.content_model_notes: Content is Page Builder widgets placed into template regions of a Stencil theme, plus Web Pages (page, link, raw HTML, contact form), blog posts, banners and script injections. A widget is a widget-template (Handlebars) plus a JSON schema for its settings and a widget instance holding the values, addressable through the V3 content APIs (/content/widgets, /content/widget-templates, /content/placements, /content/regions) - so widget CONTENT is API-accessible, but its RENDERING is the theme's Handlebars template. A headless frontend therefore does not get rendered content: it reads widget instances and must implement its own renderer per widget type, or use a visual page builder made for headless (Makeswift is the integration BigCommerce promotes) *(verify the current supported combination)*. Custom widgets are first-class - a new widget template plus schema gives merchants a drag-and-drop block in Page Builder without touching platform code. Product and category descriptions are HTML fields on the catalog resources; there is no structured content model, no content versioning and no scheduled publishing beyond what an app adds *(verify)*.
snippets.api_families_hint: see knowledge target_api_endpoint_families - three surfaces: V3 Management REST (admin, most resources), the remaining V2 REST endpoints (orders and a few legacy resources), and the GraphQL Storefront API (browser-facing, storefront tokens); plus the GraphQL Admin API for selected areas and the separate B2B Edition API host
